able to get a computer to do anything. Or perhaps we would, but it would have to be built for a single task. It's the code that enables us to take advantage of the flexibility of a computer, to get it to do whatever we want. What are the different "languages" used for? Some are fast and powerful, but difficult to use. Others aren't quite as powerful, but are much easier, making them better for beginners, but also better for writing simple software that doesn't need to do anything complicated (because it's quicker and easier to write in these simpler languages). Some are specifically designed for a particular purpose - for using in web pages, for doing mathematical tasks, for handling lots of data. Others are more general-purpose. And very often there's more than one language for doing exactly the same thing. What could one make knowing code? Every single thing your computer does, is made using code. Every single thing it ever could do, could be done by writing code to do it.',' What is code exactly? Code is a bunch of complex computer commands, each one made up of simpler commands combined in clever ways. The commands get simpler and simpler until you end up with commands like "move these bits and those bits over here and add them together." At that point, hardware takes over and moves electrical or magnetic representations of bits around between computer parts and through circuits. Languages are just sets of commands (mostly all at roughly the same level of complexity within a language, but with some variation - low and high level commands). Java and c, for instance, are similarly high level (abstracted from hardware commands), but vary in available commands, names of commands, and syntax (to some degree). Why is there code? To make it easier for people to program computers and solve problems. What are the different "languages" used for? Most languages you've heard of are general purpose languages. They are useful for most programming tasks, like desktop applications for example. Some languages are useful for manipulating graphics. Some are good at complex math. Some are good for complex logic (artificial intelligence). Some are good for parsing textlanguages. Some are good for interacting withscripting the operating system. And so on. What could one make knowing code? Lots of things. Anything you can think of that requires planning and processing information, can be programmed. Business processes are a good example. Any task you do at work, and its associated decision making, can be automated.

they deposit money in the bank, it just sits around in a vault, but that isn't the case. Enough money sits in the vault for the bank to conduct its day-to-day business, while the rest is loaned out. If someone wants to start up a business, or buy a house, they approach a bank and ask for a loan. So long as the banks don't take on a bunch of risky investments, this is fine. Actually, it's great, it's the engine of the economy. But when it goes bad, it can go REALLY bad, and that's what happened in the early 2000s. Traditionally, banks will only loan you money to buy a house if you can pay for it. They need to see that you have a certain level of monthly income and job security to ensure that you'll be able to make the payments before they'll issue you a mortgage. From 2004-2007, however, for a variety of complex reasons, the banks relaxed their lending standards, and started to issue'sub-prime' mortgages to people who were at great risk of being unable to pay them. On the face of it, this might seem like a phenomenally stupid idea and...well, it was. But there were also reasons why they might think it sounded like a good idea, in particular that housing prices at the time had been rising for a very long time, and it was taken as truth that house prices ALWAYS rise. So, the banks reasoned, since the price of the house is always going to go up anyway, in the worst case scenario where the owner is unable to make the mortgage payments, they could just take the house and not lose anything. Now, when the bank issues you a mortgage to buy a house, it's very rare that your mortgage stays with that bank. Most mortgages are sold off to other companies, who treat your debt like an asset: You owe them X amount of money, and will pay up by X time, so (simplified version) you get included on their balance sheet as X amount of money. Some investment funds started buying up mortgages and packing them together into Mortgage Backed Securities (MBS). THESE are what sunk the economy. An MBS is basically a whole bunch of mortgages packaged together, which investors can purchase. If the mortgages pay out their interest, the value of the security increases, and the investor makes money. If the mortgages default, the value of the security decreases, and the investor loses money. The idea was that by bundling a whole bunch of mortgages together, it became an extremely safe investment, because while one or two of the mortgages might default, surely enough of them wouldn't, and if they did, well, the owners could just seize and sell the house. Foolproof, right? Well, the credit ratings agencies (companies whose jobs it is to assess how safe investments are and assign them ratings based on it) thought so - they gave these MBSes their highest possible rating, because mortgage debt had always been a safe investment. And at the same time, because a lot of these mortgages were sub-prime mortgages which had high interest rates, the rate of return on these investments were extremely high. Banks got very heavily invested in Mortgage Backed Securities. They got so heavily invested, in fact, that there was a huge demand for more of them - which in turn provided incentives for banks to make even more sub-prime loans, to even riskier customers, so that they could sell the mortgages to an MBS and pocket a healthy return with (it seemed) no risk to themselves. All of this, a house of cards built on the assumption that all these mortgages couldn't possibly fail at once. Well, as it turns out, lending out hundreds of thousands of dollars to people with no steady income wasn't a great idea. A lot of sub-prime mortgages had low interest rates for the first year or so, so the problem was hidden for a while, but all of a sudden it caught up to them and in 2007 many, many of these sub-prime mortgages started to default. All those houses wound up back into the market, which greatly increased the supply of houses without any increase in demand. House prices, instead of perpetually increasing as investors had assumed, dropped precipitously as a result. Making matters worse, the drop in housing prices meant that now many of these sub-prime homeowners now owed significantly more for their mortgage than their house was actually worth, which removed any reason for them NOT to default on the debt. Suddenly, those mortgage-backed securities were worth almost nothing. This was a big problem for banks and financial firms, because they had so heavily invested in these securities that when the bubble popped, suddenly all these huge, incredibly important banks had half their balance sheet vanish out from under them. Some big banks failed, while others had to be bailed out by the government because their failure would have been catastrophic to the economy. But the damage was already done; the housing market collapsed, credit dried up so businesses couldn't get the loans they needed, and the engine of the economy stalled. And that is how the banks tanked the economy. Of course, this is a very simplified version of the story: I didn't even get into some of the more complicated stuff, like Credit Default Swaps which allowed traders to basically gamble casino-style on whether or not a mortgage security would go up or down. Also I'm not totally sure whether the banks themselves were invested in MBSes, or if they were simply left holding the bag of a bunch of terrible mortgages when the demand for new sub-prime mortgages dried up. But either way, that's the general shape of the story.

Cats only really care about food, other than that they aren't social animals in the same way as dogs. They will socialise, but only when convenient to them: so they don't need vocal cues. A cat can be trained to run towards you when you whistle, people just tend not to bother. I use a dog training clicker to tell my cats when I want them to come in, and I trained them by clicking the clicker whenever I fed the cats. They now associate that noise with food, so will come sprinting from wherever they are to get the food (unless they aren't hungry). My cats also recognise me coming into a room to stroke them from the "squeakingkissing" noise (you know that cat noise we make?) I make, and will come towards me if they want to be scratched.... but this is much less reliable than the food trigger, as they may not want to be scratched The difference is that dogs can be taught to respond to triggers for many more things than cats (attention, affection etc, rather than just food). This makes them much more reliable at responding to triggers. We also put much more effort into training dogs, and they learn based on attention: they do not instinctively come to a whistle, neither do cats. Howe both (especially when young) will come to investigate a strange noise. Again the difference is that the cat quickly learns that your whistle is not accompanied by food, so stops responding. The dog learns that you give him a stroke and attention, so comes again next time you whistle. Because we see this response, we will attempt to train the dog to do it consistently. In short, they respond differently because most people don't expect a cat to be trainable, and they don't respond to many cues so don't train them. It's not the "initial investment" that's the problem there's no reason to do them if they're not helpful. In particular: Asteroid Mining: Mining asteroids would be unbelievably expensive, and there just isn't sufficient demand for any minerals to justify the cost. That being said, there are [several startups] (URL0) devoted to developing technologies that would make such mineral extraction more cost-effective. Space Elevator: The [costs of a space elevator] (URL3) have been considered by some researchers, and such a device seems to be on the cusp of economic feasability. There are a few space elevator startups, but none of them have made the media splash that James Cameron, Larry Page, and Eric Schmidt made for their asteroid mining startup. Hydrogen Fuel Cells: Though there is ongoing research into fuel cell technology for automobiles, there would be significant infrastructure costs for transitioning to widespread use. In particular, there would need to be a nationwide network of publicly-accessible hydrogen fueling stations to replace our current gas stations. The same is true of electric cars: we would need to build a nationwide network of charging stations to make electric battery cars a viable replacement for gasoline-powered vehicles. Over the next few decades, I would guess that one of the two technologies will "win out," and electric cars currently seem to be ahead. Nuclear Batteries: I'm not sure why this is included in your list. This is fairly old technology, and several of our old spacecraft (e.g. [Voyager 2] (URL2 use a power source based on nuclear isotopes. What further applications did you have in mind? Undersea habitats and cities: Unlike some of the other technologies you cite, I'm not sure that there's any reason that we would be interested in building a large undersea habitat. This isn't about initial investment costs: once we were to build such a facility, it's hard to imagine that it would be worth the cost of supplies, staffing, and maintenance to keep it running. Purpose built cities: Again, I'm puzzled by the inclusion of this on the list. We have built a large number of [planned communities and cities] (URL1), and presumably we are in the process of constructing more. I suppose that what we as a species eventually realized is that the dreams of science fiction authors do not generally make practical goals. There is a difference between something being cool and something being useful, and we tend to think about the latter when deciding how to allocate resources. Part of this may be that, during the 1960's, the world got caught up in the fervor surrounding the space race and the dawning "space age." When the space age future failed to materialize, we learned that all of the awesome science fiction in the world doesn't make up for practical considerations about whether something is really worth the cost. I think we're glad that we went to the moon, but frankly there turned out to be not much there, and we haven't found much reason to continue going. It doesn't work to rush the future. Cellphones existed for thirty years before they became popular, and during that time almost no one bought them because they were too expensive. We had to wait for technology to improve to the point that cellphones were not only possible, but also economically viable. That's just how technology works. Once, say, a space elevator becomes a legitimately cheaper way of putting satellites into orbit, we will build one, but before that there isn't much reason to do so.', "A lot of the time it's because of politics. Something that will cost billions today with no return until twenty years later just isn't that appealing to the people making the decision today. It'll be seen as a huge dent to the budget and by the time we can see the returns, the people who made the decision probably aren't in politics anymore. Also, a lot of the things you listed sound great and look really impressive in science fiction, but they are actually a lot more complicated in reality. The feasibility of these concepts in reality may not even be understood.,Potentially good things? You want to spend my money on "potentially good?" A lot of these things could also be economy-destroying boondoggles with no payoff. The risks are huge. China has a number of empty purpose-built cities Spain has a lot of empty airports.', "Because these projects take billions of dollars, and the people interested in them usually aren't willing or able to throw that much at it.

No, at an atomic scale, is doesn't make sense to think about subatomic particles at hard objects with some defined surface that can touch another hard object with a defined surface.,Most of the time when we're talking about "splitting the atom," we're actually talking about atoms more-or-less spontaneously going through the process of [radioactive decay] (URL0). Some atoms are inherently unstable and will eventually fall apart on their own. Exactly how long that takes depends on the element we're talking about. A carbon-10 atom has a 50 chance of decaying within about 20 seconds. A hydrogen-3 atom (sometimes called "tritium has a 50 chance of decaying in a bit more than 12 years. But the point is that atoms splitting in this manner doesn't involve "touching" atoms. They'll fall apart all on their own. That said, when atoms do decay, they can throw off sub-atomic particles in addition to two smaller, complete atoms. These particles can collide with other atoms, though most of the time they don't. If it does, the affected atom will most likely immediately split. As the number of unstable atoms in a small area goes up, the odds that one of these particles will hit another unstable atom goes op. Get enough of these atoms close enough together and it can reach "critical mass," leading to a chain reaction of atomic decay and particle collisions such that a significant percentage of the mass will very rapidly decay almost all at once, releasing a potentially enormous amount of radiation. Controlled critical masses are what drive nuclear power plants. Uncontrolled critical masses are what drive nuclear weapons. Sometimes though, we really are talking about what amounts to physically hammering an atom apart. This happens in particle accelerators, where a stream of particles (atomic or sub-atomic) is magnetically accelerated to a significant fraction of the speed of light before being directed to slam into a target. Most of these particles will miss, but a few will connect, sometimes leading to atoms splitting apart.', "Even if atoms (or even the components of atoms) don't physically touch in a strict sense (as in, their spaces directly tangent) they still are connected to each other via forces. Splitting an atom evolves breaking the nucleus - an arrangement of protons and neutrons bonded together with the strong nuclear force - into two different arrangements of protons and neutrons that are each bonded together with a different amount of strong nuclear force which means some of the original bonding energy is no longer present so would be released from the atom.

The USOC sent a total of 596 athletes to Beijing (310 men and 286 women), and competed in all Olympic sports except handball.[13] The USOC selected San Jose State University in San Jose, California, as the primary processing center for all Team USA members headed for Beijing 2008.[4] They flew into San Jose via San Jose International Airport or San Francisco International Airport for at least two days of document checks, health examinations, cultural briefings, portrait sittings, uniform fittings, and last-minute workout sessions.[5] The U.S. did not win the most gold medals for the first time in a Summer Games since 1992, losing to China (51-36).[6] However, the U.S. won its most medals ever (110) in a non-boycotted games, the total medal count, and more silver and bronze medals than any other participating nation.[7] This games also marked the 8-gold medal record for U.S. swimmer Michael Phelps, who surpassed Mark Spitz's record of 7 golds in a single Olympic event in 1972.[8] Phelps also surpassed Spitz, Larisa Latynina of the USSR, Paavo Nurmi of Finland, and U.S. sprinter Carl Lewis to become the current record holder for the most Olympic gold medals (14).[9] The United States also saw milestones in women's swimming. Natalie Coughlin won 6 medals in Beijing, the most for a female Olympic swimmer.[10] Dara Torres, who won 3 silver medals after her eight-year absence, became the oldest Olympic swimmer to win a medal, at age 41.[11] Gymnast Nastia Liukin became the third U.S. female to win a gold medal in individual all-around event.[12] It was also a successful Olympics for U.S. team-based sports, as men's and women's basketball teams both won gold, as did men's volleyball, men and women's beach volleyball, women's soccer, women's eight in rowing, and the men's and women's 4x400 meter-relay teams.[13] Several other sports saw silver and bronze medals in women's volleyball, softball, baseball, both men's and women's team gymnastics, men's fencing sabre team, women's fencing foil team, and both men's and women's water polo. a plasma made of quarks and gluons. I don't know why its direction of movement would be relevant.,Regular matter, the stuff we're made of, is mostly atoms. Atoms have protons, neutrons, and electrons. Usually, the electrons are zipping around the protons and there is an equal balance of electrons (negative charge) and protons (positive charge). Basically, every electron has a "home base" which is an atom or molecule. A "regular" plasma is when you heat up matter enough that the electrons go zipping out of their home bases and you have a soup of electrons and protons and stuff all mixed together. This requires very high temperatures, like in a blowtorch or on the surface of the Sun. Turns out that if you have enough energy in one place, the protons (and neutrons) themselves will split up into even smaller bits called quarks. Gluons are particles that hold quarks together (like glue. Yes, for real.). This requires INSANE amounts of energy, but it's what we think the universe was like right after the Big Bang. All of these random quarks can reconfigure into weird types of matter, so scientists can study what comes out to see what was happening during the plasma phase. TL:DR Heat stuff up enough and it "melts" into crazy tiny particles called quarks.

never heard it called "pneumonia." We have lots of lakes, and some of them are very big. Mille Lacs, for example, is over 200 square miles, and nearly round. Most lakes freeze over during the winter; on some of them, the ice grows so thick you can drive cars on them. When the ice thaws in the spring, it melts around the edges first. So there is a period of time when you have a big floating sheet of ice that is not attached to the shore anywhere. That sheet can move. So now suppose you have a wind blowing over the surface. There may be just a tiny amount of friction between the air and the ice, but a tiny amount of force per square foot can add up to a hell of a lot of force when it's multiplied over many square miles. When the ice drifts toward shore, it builds up a huge momentum, even though the speed is very slow. The momentum can drive the ice up on shore. As you can see from the video, the ice moves very slowly, so it's not likely to injure anybody; you can easily walk away from it. The problem comes when people build their houses or cabins too close to the shore. It's like building your house on a flood plain. The ice can push in windows and doors and sometimes push houses off their foundation. But it only gets that bad on very big lakes, and it doesn't happen every year. Also, as you can see, the ice at this time is very fragile. I don't know why this happens, but when ice melts in the spring, it doesn't melt evenly. There will be pockets within the ice where it is completely melted to water, but there will still be a structure of ice that encloses it. People call this "honeycomb" ice, but the structure is not regular and geometrical like a true honeycomb; it is more random, like a rigid sponge. But you can pick up a chunk of it and crush it in your hands. It tends to get crushed while it is being pushed up on shore, so what you see is a pile of ice fragments, not a solid block of ice. It's the aggregate weight of a huge pile of ice that does the damage.

of thing linked together (think hydrocarbons like petrol). This kind of polymer can not hold information except for length (how many links in the chain). There are other kinds of polymers that link several different parts together in a chain (think RNA and DNA). Since there are different parts that each link can be made out of it can hold information (the order of chain links). Self replication is any information holding polymer that through some reaction can make other individual links link together in the same order. The problem it looks like you are having with this concept is the idea of something "dead" coming to "life." The main problem is that these two terms hold too much emotional weight. Lets call it "polymers that do not bring together other links to mimic its order" suddenly, in the presence of some catalyst, become "polymers that can attract links together in the same order as the original." Self replication is merely a reaction that attracts 'link' chemicals in a certain order then binds them together, nothing magical.','The idea that "life" - itself an unscientific and poorly defined term - came from inanimate material is called [abiogenesis] (URL1). I, on the other hand, want to address what you seem to think "life" and "death" means. A molecule "replicating" - though a characteristic seen in life - isn't the definition of life. there is also a third way, followed now only in Oman and a few isolated places in North Africa, called Khawarij. Sunnis are by far the largest group, with about 85 of all Muslims calling themselves Sunni, and make up a majority in most of the worlds Muslims countries except for Oman, Iran, Iraq, Bahrain and Azerbaijan. Shias are the next largest, about 13 of all Muslims are Shia. Khawarij are the lesser known group and much smaller, with about 1.5 million adherents around the world. So why do these three groups exist? Well it all more-or-less started on June 8th, 632, when the Prophet Muhammad, at the age of 63, died in Medina. Muhammad had successfully started a new religion, Islam, and placed himself at its head not just as a Jesus-like prophetic figure but as the political leader of all Muslims. This is radically different to say, Jesus or the Buddha because Muhammad's role was political as well as religious, leading a new and unproven state. As such, unlike some messiah wandering in the desert, he actually needed someone to follow him and take up his duties. The big question is.... who? Who could possibly follow up such an important guy - he had no sons, so no obvious successor, but someone had to lead the Muslim state. It is this question which gave rise to all 3 major sects. The Sunni View! The Prophet was defined by a few things, the most important of which was that he was pious, strong willed and technically competent. A successor couldn't just be some any old bum, divine or not, he had to be someone as close to this as possible. It needed to be someone who would be fair and just, but strong and decisive. So how do you find such a person? Elections of course! Sunnis agreed that a successor would be chosen by getting everyone together and having a big argument about who was the most righteous guy for the job. This worked quite well and was the solution used to find the first four Caliphs (Khalifa is the Arabic word for successor, hence the word Caliph) - Abu Bakr, Umar, Uthman and Ali (remember that last name, it's important!). However it didn't really work out. Though the first 4 to be elected did preside over successful times and greatly expanded the size of the Muslim nation, the fifth Caliph, who was technically Sunni, pretty much abolished the elections and made his son automatically Caliph - meaning Sunnis lost what they were fighting for yet stuck to the name and denomination. Weird, I know. The Shia View! The Prophet may have been strong willed, pious and technically competent, sure, but that wasn't just because he was a pretty cool dude! The Prophet had divine blood, he was chosen by God and man had no right to decide who was closest to him, like those blasphemous Sunnis claimed. As such, the solution is obvious, just find the person who is most closely related to the Prophet. (and is a guy, of course, it was 632 after all) The Shiites decided that the closest relative was Ali, the husband of the Prophets daughter, Fatima. Yes, that is the same Ali which the Sunnis elected to be the fourth Caliph! I told you it was complicated. The Shiites were mighty annoyed that the Caliphs were chosen by succession and campaigned hard to get Ali on the job. However things were always a bit tough for the Shia. Ali's lineage eventually died out and so they were a bit fucked, realising that there was no one left to carry on their magic bloodline hypothesis. So basically, most Shias now agree that there is no current valid successor, and define themselves by who they think the last one is. (Some Shias, called Seveners, agree that the bloodline died out after 7 generations, whereas the twelvers think it was 12) Either way, after being ignored by the Sunnis for so long they eventually developed distinct theological points, so after a while it was no longer about succession. For example, you could write something in Office365 or GoogleDocs even with no internet connection and then it would sync the next time you're online.,This is a bit of a complex question so I'll answer it as best I can. New "semantic" tags HTML5 is the next step in creating a more "semantic web," meaning that browsers can more easily tell what format certain data is in. In the past, web pages have been structured using something called "divs" (which, in code is the div tag). In order to differentiate them, most coders use an attribute within the div tag, known as "id" or "class." This is like giving a label to that div so it's known by a specific name or group. (For example: if I have a div that will serve as the header of my page, I might use the tag div id"header" .) This is all fine and well, but when a browser reads this code, it can't understand that this specific div is meant to be the header of the page. It just knows that it's called "header." In HTML5, there is actually a tag now called header . This adds "semantic value," or meaning, to the tag itself, meaning that it's easier for a browser that reads the code to know that this section is the header of a page. So, why is that important? It's for the sake of search engines like Google, who can filter through certain parts of a page when you're looking for something and improve the quality and the accuracy of your search results, making it easier for you to find what you're looking for. This same concept applies to a lot of other elements of the page. Instead of using a generic object tag that could be one of many things (images, audio, video, Flash, etc.), you can now use semantic tags called video or audio . So, instead of the browser reading the code and saying "okay, this is an object, now what type is it?," it will say "okay, this is clearly a video." The canvas tag Think about all of the fancy animations and such that Flash webpages are able to do. The canvas tag will allow web designersdevelopers to achieve many of those same effects using just HTML and JavaScript code (JavaScript being another powerful web language that works with HTML to create complex actions and applications) instead of needing to use Flash, which can be slow to load and bandwidth-heavy. Why is this a good thing? It simplifies the process of designing rich graphics and interactive elements without needing to learn and resort to a third-party technology like Flash. It's also more portable and scalable to mobile browsing, whereas Flash has had well-documented problems making the jump to smartphones. Application caching Ever been doing something on a webpage (like using an application or filling out a form) and your internet connection went out, so you lose your data and can't finish what you were doing? HTML5 solves that problem by using what's called "application caching." Basically, when the browser reads the code and comes across a tag that looks like this: html manifest"filename.manifest" .... it will read the manifest file to figure out what files a specific webapp needs to run. It will then download them and store them on your computer so that if you need to use the webapp offline, it will still function. Why is this a good thing? Obviously, it allows for a lot more flexibility in terms of how webapps are used. If you're on the go and you can't get WiFi or 3G coverage, you can still use those webapps to accomplish various things without needing an internet connection. Those are just a couple of reasons, but they're what I'd call the major ones. It's really about helping code writers write cleaner, simpler and less code, while improving HTML's capabilities and organizing data better so it's easier to sort and find. HTML5 is still in development and isn't scheduled to be finalized until around 2022, but many of its abilities are already being implemented into more progressive webpages. The drawback is that browsers don't have full capability to understand everything that HTML5 tries to do, so some of it breaks. When you're designing a webpage, you need to consider "cross-browser compatibility," meaning that you make sure the page will look the same and work the same, no matter what browser or version someone is using. Internet Explorer 6 is notoriously bad for developers because it doesn't support many of the newer features and many people (usually older people or non-computer savvy people) don't understand the importance of upgrading their browser, so web developers will need to cater to the lowest common denominator in many cases. Hope this explanation helps. I didn't cover everything, but maybe this will explain the general reason why HTML5 is a "big deal.,Facetheduke] (URL0) explains it pretty well. The other is the lysogenic or latent cycle (here on forth known as latent cycle) where it sorta hibernate for a while. if your familiar with how viruses work skip to bolded words below Viruses work in the following way: As you probably know, the central dogma of biology is DNA - - RNA protein. So DNA is the blueprint, from which a complementary transcript is made, RNA. You can think of RNA as an "easier" blueprint to read. The RNA transcript (called messenger RNA or MRNA) get read by a molecular machine called a ribosome. It instructs the ribosome on how to assemble the protein that the DNA codes for. The ribosome attaches amino acids (building blocks of protein) in the order specified by the RNA and builds up a protein which is eventually released and further modified. Proteins make up a ton of things in the body, for example things like hair and fingernails are made of protein (keratin). More importantly though, different receptors and other cellular structures are made of protein and have fundamental roles in many aspects of a cells life. All viruses are is a protein based outer coat (capsid) which surrounds the viruses DNA (or in other cases RNA) and other internal proteins. Some viruses also have a second outer coat called an envelope. Anyways, viruses work by first getting to its target site (viruses typically have attachment proteins that are complementary to cell proteins found only in certain cells). They then attach and get internalized by the cell. Other ways of infecting a cell occur but he the primary goal is to inject it's dnaRna into the cell. Now, in the case of HSV, the DNA migrates to the nucleus of the cell where many many copies of the DNA are made via hijacking the cells own DNA replication machinery. From some of these copies, an Rna transcript is generated by hijacking the cells transcriptional proteins known as polymerases. These viral Rna transcripts move to the ribosome (the molecular machines which translate the transcript into functional protein) and are translated into various proteins that are essential to the virus, such as it's capsid. When everything looks good, the viral capsid is self assembled and a copy of its DNA is packaged into it. Now this happens many times so from 1 virus infecting a cell, tons of identical viruses are made within the same cell. When too many accumulate, the virus sorta bursts open or lyses the cell and each released viruses go on to infect another cell. Often, this kills the cell, eliciting an immune response. But HSV hates the immune system, so in stead of killing the cell, it sorta just transports itself outside the cell without hurting it. What I described above is the lytic cycle. This lytic cycle produces tons of copies of the virus so it can be spread to other hosts and continue on its evolution. But your immune system is very potent and dangerous to the virus. Over the history of our species, viruses and our immune systems have coevolved many mechanisms of fighting each other. HSV has developed proteins that can impair the immune system. Other proteins it make can prevent infected cells from telling your immune cells it's infected. But the one protein your interested in is LAT-1 or the latency protein. When the immune response gets super bad, the virus decides to say fuck it, I'm gonna go sleep for a while until all this immune shit blows over. " So the virus migrate to a cluster of nerve cells known as trigeminal ganglia. Nerve cells are a safe haven, cause the immune system typically won't attack nerve cells. In nerves hsv expresses it's latency protein. This sorta shuts down any lytic genes that would be involved in infecting cells, and instead sorta makes the virus hibernate until safer times. During times when your immune system is suppressed (certain drugs, HIV infections, and stress can suppress immune system) the virus somehow realizes this and reactivates itself and it's lytic genes. The virus leaves the nerves, and goes on to infect more cells. The virus also sheds at this point, meaning it's contagious. (idk for sure if latent HSV is contagious or not). Anyways, sorry for the long answer. I love talking about the brilliant nature of viruses. If you asked this question in preparation for finals in couple weeks, I hope I help you.

Blue eyes indicate absence of melanin, it is a structure that happens to just scatter the light to appear blue. Similar to blue bird feathers, Morpho butterfly wings, the sky and the sea (Not identical mechanisms) Black eyes are chock full of melanin. Inbetween you have gradients of dilution of melanin, with green being the underlying structural blue with a very slight yellow smattering of melanin, mixing it to appear green; hazel being a bit more, so the warm yellow aspect is stronger, etc. You inherit the instructions for how much melanin (and pheomelanin which is light red) you produce. Your parents have different amounts and versions of the genes carrying these instructions, written into DNA, which is bunched into chromosomes. Humans have usually two sets of chromosomes. During meiosis (when egg cells and sperm cells are created), chromosomes get split up and the DNA untangled, then there's some swapping between corresponding chromosomes with a chance of deletion or duplication, so you get a pretty random half of their genes and some extra variation, too! When an egg and sperm cell unite, there's again some crossing over between the chromosomes the sperm and those the egg brings. And in the end, you get a random mixture of what the parents have in THEIR genes. It can be pretty surprising, one parent might have donated more copies than one of a melanin-producing gene so a child might have a trait as strong as that parent, or get only a fraction of it. (I'm the tanning, blond haired, blue eyed white dragon of a darker-skinned black-haired brown-eyed guy and a green-eyed, very pale and sunburning mother because my dad had an extra copy of "no melanin, please" lying around that I got, but was overshadowed in him by his melanin-producing genes) All this means that you can approximately, but never with 100 certainty calculate the odds of producing offspring with a certain eye and skin color. (Skin color is also partly linked to the sex chromosome X.) ', "There are some traits that blend, rather than select one or the other. Which traits do this seems to vary from one species to another. Is the fuel good fuel? oxygenated blood. Can the fuel get to the engine obstructed blood flow Is the spark plug good? brain damage','It all depends on what is happening during cardiac arrest that indicates whether your heart can be shocked or not. There are two main "shockable rhythms," ventricular tachycardia and ventricular fibrillation. To understand these, you need to understand how the heart normally works. The top of the heart is called the atria (plural for atrium). There is a location in the right atrium called the SA node. This is the "pacemaker" of the heart. It generates an electrical signal that travels through special fibers from the top of the heart to the bottom (the ventricles). This progression causes the atria to contract, filling the ventricles, and then the ventricles contract, pumping blood to the lungs and rest of the body. In ventricular tachycardia (V-tach), the ventricles are squeezing on their own and not waiting for the impulse from the SA node to cause contraction. While it's possible for this rhythm to continue to pump blood effectively, often it is not. Either the contractions aren't strong enough to pump the blood effectively or not enough time is allowed for the heart to fill up, so it's only half full when it pumps again. So shocking this type of rhythm somewhat "resets" the whole heart and stop the irregular heartbeat. In ventricular fibrillation (V-fib), the individual muscle cells in the ventricles are not contracting together. They're just all firing randomly all the time. So since there is no organization to the contractions, the heart just quivers and does not beat. Shocking, again, resets all these cells and hopefully allows for an organized contraction initiated by the SA node. There are dozens of other rhythms or arrhythmias that are unshockable. The most common misconception is that someone in asystole (no heart muscle activity at all), also known as flatline, can be fixed with shocking. Since there is no electrical activity to "reset" shocking does nothing. The only thing that can possibly help is high-quality CPR and ACLS drugs like epinephrine, amiodarone or vasopressin.', "DOI: UK physician in anaesthesia and intensive care. When you have a cardiac arrest, it is caused by one of two problems, either there is a mechanical problem (for example, the muscle is failing, or there's not enough blood to pump) or an electrical problems (abnormal heart rhythm) Using a defibrillator attempts to reset electrical problems. It has no effect on the muscle (mechanical) side of things. As such, it can only be used in specific circumstances. Most cardiac arrests are caused by mechanical issues and therefore a defib can only be used in a small proportion of patients. Mechanical issues can only be fixed by addressing the cause, for example, replacing lost circulating blood. The muscle can be forced to beat harder by drugs like adrenaline. If the muscle itself is failing or dead, then usually it is fatal.," "A defibrillator literally does what its name is: It stops (atrial or ventricular) fibrillation. Fibrillation is when the heart muscles are contracting rapidly and irregularly (basically like shivering) and due to this the heart doesn'tcan't pump blood anymore (but the muscles and electrical system of the heart still work). The electical shock from the defibrillator stops all contraction so when the shock is over the contraction starts again synchronized and the function is reset. When there is no heart movement at all (asystole'flatline'; 80 of cases are the result of previous fibrillation) that means that there is much more wrong with your heart because neither the electrical system nor the muscles are currently working. In that case only CPR in conjunction with adrenaline may work to actually restart the heart but this works in less than 20 even in a hospital. Unless there is an obvious cause that can be fixed this situation will most likely end in death.

Most of the consumer market doesn't have a significant alternative to whichever ISP is available in their area. Net NeutralityCommon Carrier Status for Internet In essense, the FCC is ruling that Internet providers are to be considered common carriers. This means that the providers can't discriminate with respect to what traffic they carry. All traffic must be treated the same way, regardless of where it is going, where it is coming from, and what it contains. This is happeneing because the ISPs have demanded payment from third-party services such as Netflix to improve their connectivity to the end-users. Simultaneously, various forms of preferential treatment have been given to services owned by, or affiliated with, the various ISPs. On a side note, I'm particularly irritated over the idea that my ISP has demanded Netflix pay to be brought to me, because I was pretty sure that this is what I was paying them for. WiFi Blocking Mariott hotels run a for-pay WiFi network for their guests and conferees. The rate that they charge for conferees is extortionate, being a 3-4 digit price per device per day. Obviously, people would prefer to use their own portable hot spots (Mi-Fi or similar device) and Mariott's response was to jam such devices. They were fined for this. The FCC later clarified their position that it is altogether not permissible to jam WiFi deliberately. Hope this helps.

Being the driver and having control of the movement can be even better 3d movies can be the opposite for some people. Your brain thinks you should be moving, but your body is stationary. Looking of the screen at an exit sign or a seat back recalibrates you.', "When the ground in front of you is heading toward you rapidly, the things you see don't change as much as things to either side. You see a far-off tree, then the tree is closer, then it's right there, and then - assuming you didn't drive right into it - it is gone. Your brain has plenty of time to capture and assimilate data, to figure out how stuff is moving relative to you and, based on that information, how important each thing you see is (in terms of your goal, which is often'getting where you are going in one piece'.). You have time to understand what you are seeing, so you feel okay. Things to the side zip by so fast that sometimes we don't have time to even know what we are seeing, and we definitely don't have time to process the visual information with our brains.... by the time our brains have figured out one thing, a few hundred other things have gone last at high speed. This inability to get a mental grasp on what we are looking at (to either side) can make us feel like the ground is slipping out from underneath us, which it is, technically. Vertigo, nausea, motion sickness.... these are all just feelings of un-ease caused by not being able to grasp what we see before it is far behind us. Our brains plus our visual acuity let us know howwhere we stand in relation to everything else. When we are moving, signals from our inner-ear - the seat of balance - help us understand what we are seeing. This can lead to some weird experiences, like when you're stopped at a light and the car next to you starts rolling backwards and you think it's you that is moving.... the information from your eyes and the information from your inner-ear don't match, and you have a moment of panic trying to figure out what is really going on. When you are moving, the road ahead is less likely to contain elements that cause such disparity in our senses.... but looking to the side, that's almost all we see. Focusing on the horizon, which doesn't really change much, instead of focusing on the things zipping by near the vehicle, can reduce or eliminate ill-at-ease feelings like motion sickness. This is such a fundamental process that it even happens when we are not moving, but we are seeing other things move. When filming trains, for instance, the train needs to go faster when it is coming toward the camera or it looks like less of a threat - not much changes from one moment to another - but filming from the side, the train needs to go slower or all we see is motion blur. Filming a train going its normal speed results in images that make us feel something is not right.... adjusting the speed of the train based on the direction it is being filmed helps the image match up with what our eyes, brains, and inner-ear think is happening.

Is this really common for most people?','The brain is extremely complex and we have retained several of our defensive mechanisms from our early beginnings when survival was more reliant on instinct and the fight or flight response was much more dominant than it is today. So we basically still have these powerful self preservation instincts that kick in when our brain thinks we are in danger. The problem is that the part of the brain that deals with this is much faster than the part of the brain that can process all the information being received and recode it into a message we can understand. So part of our brain has picked up on signs of danger or signs that there is no danger. Someone touching you, especially in a crowded place, is an automatic sign of danger. However, when it's someone we know even if we can't see them our brain picks up on other clues such as their smell, the sound of the way they walk, maybe other sounds that your brain associates with them but you don't, and in the case of people you are very close to even their touch. The self preservation part of your brain can pick up on this clues instantly before the other part of your brain can translate the information into a message you can understand. Generally you will see the person before the brain creates the message and sight is one of the fastest senses so you then have confirmation of your self preservation instincts. This is basically where the "sixth sense" comes from. It's not an extra sense but parts of your brain picking up on clues and processing information faster than your brain can tell you what is going on. The goose bumps are a self preservation instinct when your body thinks you are in danger and there are no other clues to cancel this instinct. TL;DR - Your brain can pick up on other clues that tell you if the person you can't see is a stranger or not and the self preservation part of the brain reacts faster than it can translate the information to you. commonwealth is no different than a state but the name was chosen to be used in place of state. For example Massachusetts is a Commonwealth, New York is a State, both are considered defined legal areas for local jurisdiction.,There is no significant difference between a krai and an oblast, both on a legal level as well as in practice. Republics have more legal rights, in that they can define their own official languages and have their own constitution and legislature. Russia is legally the Russian Federation, so these republics are nation states within the Russian Federation. In the Russian constitution, republics are defined as states and are meant to be regions for certain ethnic minorities. So the Chechen Republic (or Chechnya) is a federal subject of the Russian Federation, and yet it has its own official language, government, constitution, legislature and an ethnically non-Russian majority of the population. It is much like a state in itself, so much so that someone from Chechnya would be called Chechen, not Russian. There are also autonomous okrugs, which have a predominant ethnic minority and some improved legal rights, including the ability to participate in international and federal agreements and contracts independently. Moscow and Saint Petersburg function as separate federal subjects (federal cities).

its own. To put an object in orbit, it must go very fast, so that rather than falling towards earth, it goes around. For example, the space station is at 200-250 miles of altitude. There is still about 90 of the earth gravity at that altitude. The only reason that it doesn't fall down is its orbital speed, which is 17,500mph! Theoretically, you don't have to go in orbit. You can go straight up, as slowly as you like, but you will have to constantly fight gravity, which requires a lot of energy.," "It doesn't. A rocket could rise into the sky at basically any speed, as long as it could keep burning enough fuel. When they start to lift off, they're not going fast. As a rocket pushes fuel down, it pushes the rocket up. All it has to do is exceed the force of gravity by a little bit, and it will rise. When a rocket goes fast, that means it's exceeding the force of gravity by a lot. If we shot spaceships into space with catapults or cannons or something, and they didn't have rockets to keep pushing them up, they'd have to start out quite fast: fast enough to escape the pull of gravity before they fell back. That's because they wouldn't have anything pushing them up as they rose, so they'd have to start out with all the energy they'd need to break free. At the surface of the earth, gravity pulls with a constant force, but as you get farther away from earth, the pull is weaker. So if you shot something into the air fast enough, it could get far enough away that the force of gravity wasn't enough to pull it back to earth. However, in practice, this has never happened. No one has ever built a catapult or cannon that strong and shot something into space with only that initial force. So, spaceships blast off with rockets.," "Quite simply: gravity. It's pretty strong, and escaping it's pull requires a lot of force.

left. It's all been broken down and mixed in with the water so what you see coming into the plant's pump house is just grey water with debris mixed in. (toilet paper is also dissolved and mixed in as well.) At this point, the water is run through various different screens (the kind used depends on the plant.), but essentially all the water runs through this and the larger matter is separated from it and emptied into a dumpster or other waste storage. From here, as far as my plant operated, the water is stored in a giant holding tank so it can be processed through the plant at a steady pace. From the tank, the first area it would go in my plant (this is different in other plants who use different treatment methods) is the belt press. The water is taken onto a machine that has a system of rollers holding a large, very tightly wound belt. All of the debris is pulled out from the water and is removed on a conveyor belt to the outside where it is collected in a large dumpster. This is shipped out to be later made into plastics or fertilizer. After that the water is collected and sent to a large aeration container where it is stored in these large pools that have air passed into them periodically throughout the day. The purpose of this is that a coli form which likes the feed on the matter in the water is attracted to it and helps break it down which aids in the process of sanitizing the water. This bacteria is actually extremely important and it must be checked multiple times a day to ensure that the levels of bacteria are neither too high or too low. The pH balance must also be checked as well, if it gets too high the bacteria will die off. Anyway, at this point the final destination of the water (again in my plant we used this but other plants have different methods) is the UV chamber. This is another large basin that fills and then is screened through the UV chamber once it reaches a certain height. The water passes through a small channel here which has a number of high powered UV lights destroying any remaining bacteria in the water. This chamber is also where a lot of grease balls end up and why I hate when people pour grease down there drains. The grease balls were usually nto caught by the screen and survive all the way to this chamber where we had to manually fish them out. At this point a couple of things can happen. The water can be emptied out into a natural stream, sent to the towns water works where it is redistributed or both. Hope this is helpful!,Modern day treatment can been seen [here] (URL0). Our ancestors used a variety of methods ranging from just dumping it in a river in rural areas, to complex sanitation systems built by the Romans. Essentially the idea is always to get the waste to water and let it wash away.

cause a change in personality.','This is a super broad question, so I can only give a broad answer. Medications are purposefully designed or naturally existing compounds (tiny bits of material) which can be recognized by our body. Our body has a HUGE amount of chemical signaling; practically every part of our body needs to communicate with another. The catch is that the signals are very specific, and the cells who can "accept" the signal have very specific areas on them to accept a perfectly fitting chemical (Signal). When something has bound to this area on the cell it causes what is called a cascade, a mutliple step process which gives instructions to various parts of our body (which can target one cell, or many cells, to produce something, to stop something, or to control something). Medications are implemented to bind to these specific signals areas on our cells, in specific areas of our body. Due to the fact cells often have specific receptors for these chemicals (either man-made, natural, or through our own production), we are able to "force a change" in someones body through their own internal environment. For personality changes, the cascade and specificity are critically important. Your body is wired so that all the organs and systems work together - adjusting one will often affect the other. Medications that target your brain will directly affect your personality, because these medications are telling your cells to behave a certain way by the sheer purpose of the drug. Moreover, medications which affect other systems, such as your cardiovascular system, can cause nutrients to move around your body faster (higher heart rate seen in coffee, for instance), which can force your brain to deal with an abnormal amount of desired nutrients for that cell (usually accidentally entering the cell through gradients). Your internal environment is being forced to behave in a specific way, and your body reacts to that change by sometimes making your personality change.','All that is you, and your personality is nothing but bio chemical reactions in the brain. By adding new or foreign chemicals to the brain you can alter these reaction and change you.','Your brain works through a series of electrical and chemical reactions. Medications are chemicals, and some of them directly interfere with (or help) the chemical reactions that take place in your brain. Since your personality is mainly the result of what your brain is doing, anything that affects its function may affect your personality. To take a simple example, consider someone who has a very lazy and sleepy personality. Now boost the overall rate of signals in their brain, and they are likely to seem more alert, excited, and energetic.','They can either deplete or increase the amount of neurotransmitters in the brain. Different amounts of different neurotransmitters affect many things, such as behavior and emotions, which can change their personality

Two people with BAC of 0.05 might behave much more differently. 3) Alcohol metabolism, aka how quickly does your body process alcohol and turn it into less dangerous stuff (acetaldehyde and then acetate). Alcohol is absorbed in about 30-90 minutes (generally 30 min though). At that point, it is in your blood and shows up in BAC tests. While alcohol is in your stomach, it isn't causing any drunken effects. Imagine having a propane tank. It isn't doing anything in the tank. But as it leaks out into their air (bloodstream) it spreads and affects our brains. That is why vomiting shortly after drinking is an effective defence by your body. A lot of alcohol is removed from the body and won't make it to the bloodstream. About 20 of alcohol can be converted in the stomach through a process called MEOS. So if you have 10 ml of pure alcohol, only 8 ml might make it into your blood stream. Interesting as you drink more often and in high quantities, your body produces more of the stuff needed for the MEOS process. This leads to more alcohol being broken down in the stomach before it ever reaches your blood. Less alcohol in blood means less BAC and less drunk. As well, some people have almost no enzymes needed for MEOS, which means that almost all alcohol they consume makes it to the bloodstream unconverted. Volume of blood increases with weight. For a 200-pound, six-foot male, the blood volume is estimated at 7 liters, For a 100-pound, five-foot female, the estimate is 3.5 litres. bigger bathtub more water. Assuming the same volume of ethanol is absorbed into the blood, a 200 pound person will have roughly half the BAC of a 100 pound person. Put 5 drops of dark food colouring into 1 litre, and 5 drops of dye into 2 litres. Obviously the amount of dye is the same, but the effect of the dye is greatly reduced and the two litres is less dark. Once it gets into your bloodstream, it can get into your brain and start screwing stuff up. This leads to alcohol symptoms such as balance issues, mood changes, etc. Visible drunkenness As you drink more and more often, your brain gets better at functioning normally despite the alcohol. Imagine getting on a boat and trying to walk around on rough seas with the captain. He is much more stable than you, and appears unaffected by the waves. By being at sea a long time, they have gotten better at compensating for the boats movements. The brain learns to function and adapts to work with alcohol present. This is why chronic drinkers are able to perform tasks normally with high BACs whereas occasional drinkers "appear" more drunk. This is also why chronic drinkers may suffer from mood changes and problems when they aren't drunk, like that sea captain coming back to land and struggling to regain his "land-legs." Lastly, alcoholics seem to break down alcohol in the bloodstream differently. While they convert alcohol to acetaldehyde at similar speeds to non-alcoholics, they don't convert that into the less harmful acetate (which gets converted into water and CO2 and removed). That slower breakdown means that there is much more acetaldehyde in their system. That chemical is pretty bad, and does things like create special opioid like chemicals in the brain (addiction), wrecks organs, etc. I am wondering if one of the reasons alcoholics end up as alcoholics is because they don't feel as sick and uncomfortable as nonalcoholics tend to be after a number of drinks. Recently however things like the rising number of Japanese alcoholics (who can get drunk after 1-2 drinks because of missing enzymes), the discovery of alcohol allergies in alcoholics (wheatrye allergies) and alcoholics perseverance through reverse tolerance suggest this isn't the case. around a magnet, which induces a current that we can record and playback as sound. The problem with dynamic mics is that they aren't very sensitive, so they don't pick up quiet sounds very well. The solution is to use a condenser mic. It's called a condenser because in British English the word "condenser" is the same as the American word "capacitor." A capacitor is an electrical component where there are two plates separated by some material and then charged. A condenser or capacitor microphone works by charging one of the plates (which means a condenser mic has to be powered, dynamics do not need a power source), and then one of the plates is free to move with sound, which changes the capacitence, which we can use as a signal. The thing is you can make those plates very, very small and out of very light materials, which makes them much more sensitive. The pro of a condenser is it allows us to record softer sounds a lot better, which makes them great as studio mics. The con is it picks up everything we don't want a lot better than a dynamic. You tend to use dynamics in places with loud sounds where you don't want room noise or any bleed, like in a live concert or in a noisey environment that you can't control.

To keep this ELI5, I won't explain monetary policy or anything like that beyond just to say how the Fed does this and why. There are a couple of big functions of the Fed, and all of them focus on one of the Fed's two "Dual Mandates" (or, arguably, a third goal I'll explain in a second). The Dual Mandates are to create fiscal policies that promote "maximum employment" (meaning 'as many people have jobs as possible or "controlled inflation" (meaning 'prices don't rise out of control. If you don't know much about economics, cover your ears because I'm going to spoil Macroeconomics 101 for you: you can't give everyone jobs AND have low inflation. Employment and inflation are tied together: when one goes up, so does the other. The "Dual Mandate" is really just a way to articulate the third, over-arching goal: to keep the economy stable. To not let one rise so much that it causes the other to get out of whack. So that's why the Fed does everything it does: either to control unemployment, or to control inflation but always to keep the economy stable. Sowhat does the Fed do? - It's the "bank's bank." This came into play a lot during the bank bailouts, which I'll get to in a second, but it also has a more routine effect on the economy too: under the Fed is a system called the Check Clearing System. I won't get into how it works, because it's needlessly complicated for our purposes, but the important thing is that before it came around, when times were economically rough, your bank might not accept a check that I wrote to you from my account at my bank. Banks couldn't be sure the money was in my account, and they didn't want to have to sue my bank to get the money, and they didn't want to piss you off by putting money in your account and then having to remove it when it turned out that my check wasn't good. So the Fed acts as a neutral go-between between the banks involved in a check transaction (which is why checks take a couple of days to clear), and the result is that if you write a check to somebodyno matter where they do their bankingthey'll be able to cash it. - It can give banks huge sums of money very quickly. This, of course, sounds like a bad idea. But remember: one of the goals the Fed has is to keep the economy stable. And if banks stop trusting that other banks have enough money to pay them, they will clam up and stop doing business with them, which will stop the economy in its tracks. So if it looks like a huge bank might go bust because it can't borrow enough to cover its debts, the Fed can become the "Lender of Last Resort," which basically just means that... - It can create money. This is probably the most powerful thing the Fed can do because it violates every rule about money there is. If you want to get 10 to buy something, you need to get it from someone else, but that person had to get it from someone, and that someone had to get it from someone else, and so on. Everybody gets money from someonebut not the Fed. The Fed is the first step in this chain: it made that 10 out of thin air. You asked earlier how the Fed works with banks, and this is a big way: part of the way that Check Clearing System I mentioned earlier works is that each bank that participates in it (which is pretty much all of them, because why would you want to open an account with a bank you can't take other banks' checks to?) has an account with the Federal Reserve (which is not unlike your account at your bank in that it has a account balance). Now, the Fed can create money in two ways: it can walk over to a Federal Mint (like the ones in Philadelphia or San Fransisco) and literally ask them to print the amount of money it wants, or it can go into the accounts banks have with the Fed and change the amount of money in the account to a higher number. When banks wake up the next morning and see that they have more money than they thought, they'll immediately start lending it out (because banks want to lend moneyit's how they make money!) and that gets the economy's gears moving. Using this second way, the Fed can create and move huge sumstrillions of dollarsin just a few minutes. The fact that the Fed can magically save a bank before it goes under can be used to avert a bank panicwhich is one of the forces which worsened the Great Depression, and, again, this all speaks to the Fed's goal to keep the economy stable. - It can set interest rates. Most of the time, when the Fed creates money, it lends it out to banks. So say the Fed decides to create 1 billion today. It says to a couple of banks "you can have this money, but you have to pay me back at 3 interest." The banks say "Sure! I'll borrow it from you, and then turn around and lend it to my customers at 5 and keep the profits!" And then the Fed would add the money to the bank's account. Bam! 1 billion created. The Fed can affect interest rates throughout the entire country by raising and lowering the interest rate it offers banks, because banks will lend at the lowest rate they can function at (because otherwise, you, the customer, would go to a bank that offers a lower rate and the bank misses out on getting interest from you), so the Fed can directly affect the interest rate you get on your home or car loan or your student loanor whatever sort of loan you went to your bank to get just by affecting the "overhead" cost the bank has to pay to get the money in the first place. These last two monetary powers are big ones because they can be used to target those Dual Mandates. If it prints lots of money, the banks will lend it out and people will use that to hire new employeesthat lowers unemployment but it also artificially increased the money supply so each dollar is "worth" less (which is just another way to think about what inflation is). There's a lot of math and economics that go into when the Fed uses any of these things, but it isn't really necessary to know about the specifics to understand why the Fed does what it does unless you want to know why it chose to create the amount of money it did, or why it chose a specific bank to loan to, etc.','a few people have answered this one already... become a Member of Parliament (MP), i.e. they have to get elected to the legislative body. Then they have to be selected as the head of their party. Then their party has to be able to control a majority of the votes in Parliament or lead a coalition of parties that can reach that majority. Then the Queen, who is the official head of state, appoints the leader of that party as Prime Minister (PM), who is head of government, and then the Prime Minister appoints Cabinet Ministers. (Another difference from the US: in the US, the President is both head of state and head of government.) That's "forming a new government." Another difference from the US: it happens all at once. There's no scenario in the US where every elected official is up for re-election at the same time because the Senators only come up for election every 6 years on a staggered basis. So during any presidential election year, the President, all of the House of Representatives, and only 13 of the Senate is up for election, but 23 of the Senate isn't up for re-election. In a UK general election, though, the whole government is up for re-election at once. Which is part of why the US would never refer to an election as "forming a new government," but the UK would. Several things can trigger an election in the UK Parliament: One has to happen every 5 years, so every MP, including the PM, is up for re-election every 5 years A majority of Parliament votes "no confidence" in the current government, in which case there's a grace period to get a new coalition together, and, if that doesn't happen, a general election must be held A vote of 23 of Parliament can decide to throw out the current government and hold a general election to elect or re-elect the government. That last one is what Theresa May did recently, because she thought her party could pick up seats in Parliament by having another election less than a year after the last one. She was wrong, and nearly lost control of the government, and probably permanently undermining her own power.', "Just to add, the Queens role in this is purely ceremonial. Officially she dissolves government, etc, but she does so on the basis that if she didn't do as Parliament wanted they would just get rid of her.,It's just the jargon of parliamentary systems. The equivalent term in the U.S. would be "administration;" it includes the head of government and all the associated cabinet positions and other appointed posts.

have a sample from a population. The sample will have some sort of distribution (In many real world cases, this distribution is Normal, as seen [here] (URL0). If you are interested in why, ask and ye shall receive!), but not always. Sometimes, a particular distribution is skewed from the middle, or away from being normal. For example, an [f-distribution] (URL1) is used to determine the effectiveness blocking has on treatment variances. Every distribution has its uses, and the one that obviously has implications to your work is the Beta distribution. Now, look at the first link, the normal curve. You see how there are percentages that correspond to sections of the curve? That's the probability that, given a sample with that distribution (In this case, a normal distribution), if you pick any particular point it will fall in that range. (That's actually a poor technical definition, but you can think of it like that). So, pick a random point, and you have a 0.1 chance that it will fall three standard deviations from the mean. (The lower case sigma is the standard deviation, and is a way of measuring the variability of your data). The beta distribution is definitely one of the more esoteric ones as an undergrad I haven't actually used it in any real world applications, just proofs. However, what its actual use is isn't very important, as we're just looking to determine what this function does. So, let's talk about another function in Excel first, BETADIST. This returns a probability, p, that a sample point in a beta distribution has of being below or equal to that point. The BETADIST function has parameters alpha, beta, A, and B. Alpha and beta are statistics parameters, and they are used to define the mean and the variance (Average and squared-deviation from the average) of the beta distribution. A and B are the scale that it is put to, with A less than B. The A and B are not needed, they are defaulted to 0 and 1 as it is in a standard beta distribution. So, BETADIST looks for a point, and gives a probability. (Just like in the normal curve, the point would have been 3sigma, and the probability would be 0.001). So, what does BETAINV do? The opposite! You put in a probability, and it returns the point at which it has that probability of being in less than or equal to that point. So, BETAINV (p, alpha, beta, A, B) returns a point, X, that does exactly that.

a VERY clear link from A to B, and one must also define a very clear link from B to A. For example, let's try to say that "Running out of gas causes your car to stop." Then, through sample testing we'd get a very high (Read: 100 in this case) correlation from your car running out of gas, to your car stopping. That is enough to prove a correlation. How to prove causation? By proving the contrapositive. Prove through sampling that if a gar is NOT stopped, then it is NOT out of gas (Which you can, again, see with 100 certainty. In a simple case, by doing this, you would prove a causation. In complicated cases with dozens or even hundreds of variables (For example, the effect that a government mandated health care system would have on the economy) there is absolutely no way to prove a causation, only a high correlation.','The key is to show that the "effect" must be preceded by the prescribed "cause." So in your testing you try to demonstrate that the "effect" does not occur as a result of other likely causes or no cause at all. When being peer reviewed, the reviewers, who are usually expert in the field, may propose alternative possible causes, and the original investigator (s) will have to address those possibilities. In science one never "proves" anything unless you are showing something to be false. The positive case for a cause- effect argument is made by the asserting the hypothesis and supporting it with tests that seem the most likely to show it false, but which fail to do so.','I hate this phrase. Correlation is a necessary but not sufficient condition for causation. Which means correlation very often does imply causation. You just need addition evidence. Evidence that A causes B includes: Correlation - B happens when A happens Negated correlation - B does not happen when A does not happen Isolation - possible casual agents C, D, and E have been eliminated Chronology - A happens before B happens Mechanism - A does this one thing to cause B Remember, philosophers still debate whether there even is such a thing as causality. The best scientists can do is show high and isolated correlation with a well understood mechanism.

If the jury thinks that you probably did it, but they're not convinced beyond a reasonable doubt, then they will find you not guilty. Civil matters are separate from crimes. They're where you've damaged somebody in some way, and the person who was damaged wants to be paid back for it so they file a lawsuit. This is where I was hit by the car when you were driving drunk and I want you to pay my medical bills and fix my car. I can't send you to jail, I just want my money. The name of the case is Pxalt v. OP. To get my money, I need to prove to a jury that you injured me because of your negligence, and I need to prove it to that jury by a preponderance of the evidence a fancy way of saying that I need to prove that you probably did it, or that you most likely did it. If the jury is convinced that far, then they'll find that you have to pay me. So as you can see, these are separate matters with separate parties, separate goals, and separate burdens of proof. But by committing the one act (driving drunk), you opened yourself up to liability on both tracks. In the case of OJ Simpson, the criminal jury found him not guilty because they weren't convinced beyond a reasonable doubt that he did it. However, the civil jury was satisfied that he probably did it. And so for the civil jury, that was enough to impose liability on him.', "He was found [liable] (URL0) for the deaths, but he wasn't found guilty of committing it. Very good explanation in the link. Basically there's a different standard for evidence in a criminal court vs a civil suit, where there's more pressure for the evidence to substantiate the specific charges being brought in a criminal court in full for you to be sent to prison, as opposed to how you can basically be found mostly at fault in a civil suit and have to pay up.,In a criminal court, the prosecution needs to prove beyond a "reasonable doubt" that the defendant was guilty. In the eyes of a juror, that's like 99. In a civil court the plaintiff, or person bringing the suit against the defendant, only needs to get to that 51 mark in the eyes of the juror. If they can show that it was more likely than not that the defendant was responsible then they win.

Fitness in the evolutionary sense is "likelihood of passing on genes." It is something different every year, every place, every biological niche. Often it is a combination of the ability to survive for a long time, mate a lot, or produce healthy offspring in a safe environment. Living socially and in groups provides all three of those. That's one reason you can argue that empathy increases fitness. There are countless others. It is, also, a common misconception that evolution makes unnecessary traits disappear.
