I will, however, try and answer from an Australians perspective. For Australia and New Zealand, I think the true roots of this'near-hero worship' of our soldiers, or'diggers' as they are called in Australia, came from World War I. More specifically, the battle of Gallipoli. Before this battle, the soldiers of both these nations had never quite taken part in a true, nation defining battle or war. And with the outbreak of World War I, Australia and New Zealand formed the ANZAC's, the Australian and New Zealand Army Corpse. This is particularly significant as it was the first time both the Australians and the New Zealander's fought together, side by side. The main role they served in the war was to capture the Ottoman post that sat there. This move was actually co-ordinated by the British, who were planning to use the post to stage an offensive on Constantinople. However the operation did not go to plan. The Ottoman forces dug themselves in, and managed to hold off the allied forces, leading to an eventual victory after 8 months of fighting. This battle for the ANZAC's, quite simply, was an absolute bloodbath. Because of the trench warfare style of war used in WWI, the ANZAC's were dug into the side of the hill and basically couldn't move forward. This lead to many attempted charges up over the hill and into the enemy trench line. However because of the well positioned Ottoman machine guns and trenches overlooking the ANZAC position, it meant that the ANZAC's stood no chance, and were mowed down time and time again. What came from this are the stories of great heroism surrounding these soldiers, who would run into open battle where almost certain death awaited them, and yet they continued to try again and again. The battle played an enormous role in forging the national identities of these two countries; these two small island nations on the other side of the world, fighting side by side, tooth and nail, for their countries and for their Queen. Their tremendous heroism is echoed every year on ANZAC day, where veterans of both countries parade in their cities, and remember the fallen.," "The Ancient Greek and Roman cultures seem to have taken military service as a sign of good moral character, and the fact that soldiers could be seen as selfless has often encouraged a view of them as heroes. For governments, it is also politically useful for soldiers to seem like the good guys, because they're doing what the government wants them too (so the government might look better, too). The armed forces themselves also encourage this sense of heroism, because it can help troops' morale and recruitment.

an invaluable resource for a company of all sizes to get advice from more experienced people in the field, or just at managing a company. It is not uncommon for executives of companies in the same field, but not directly competing, to sit on the board of a company. When getting started in such a cut throat world, someone always available to ask for advice or to simply yank your chain when you are about to go off the deep end can save the company. Technically, the founders start out as the board of the company, and as they seek out investors, the investors typically want a place on the board themselves, or the ability to name someone to the board. They do this so they can have some form of control in their sizable investment. They can even force a founder to step down from the CEO position in favor of someone with more experience. (This is not uncommon, as it is extraordinarily rare for someone to possess the skills to both successfully start a company and the skills to run it once it has grown.) It is also important to note that while a founder can be fired, heshe still retains any ownership they have in the company. Board members can get this voting power, because when you seek out investors, you typically give very large portions of the company to your investors in return for their investment. Hence the concept of a "valuation." This is getting into investing, but the short version is that when you ask an Angel Investor for 2 million, he may ask for 50 of your company because the company is only worth a total of 4 million. When seeking out a Venture Capital firm, a company like Spotify can ask for 400 million at a 4 billion valuation and only give away 10 of their company (and 10 of their votes). So, we'll say the owner is now at the point where the company is valued at 100 million, but their share has been diluted down to 10, thus they only get 10 of the vote. If all the board members vote to kick him out as the CEO, he's got to go, because he no longer controls the majority of the company. He still has a net worth of 10 million, they can't take that away, but now he is simply an owner of the company instead of an owner who happens to be the CEO. He still gets his 10 vote, and if he can convince a majority of the owners (in percentages) to vote him back in as CEO, he's right back on top.', "When Zuckerberg took the company private he owned only 28.2 of the company. If he wanted to have complete control he should have not have given (or sold) ownership of the company to others. But that would have meant he wouldn't have had the money or resources to grow the company.

The geometry of bicycles and motorcycles means that leaning them causes them to steer. Gyroscope effects are sometimes mentioned here too, but it has a lot to do with the shape of the tire. The edge is shorter, and therefore moving slower, than the center of the tire. When leaned, the center wants to cover more ground and "catch up" with the side of the tire. This causes the bike to turn. The turning of the bike makes it straighten up, due to a moving object's tendency to keep moving in a straight line (when turning, it leans to the outside of the curve). Once it straightens up, it stops turning. So you might notice a small deviation from a straight line but it's not going to continue turning. The correction is self-limiting and when you're moving these "corrections" are so quick and constant it just feels like a force or natural tendency for the bike to stay upright.','Minute Physics did a video about it. [Here it is] (URL0). tl;ds: In short a normal bicycle is stable thanks to a combination of: - the front wheel touching the ground behind a backwards tilted steering axis, - the center of mass of the front wheel and handlebars being located in front of the steering axis, - and the gyroscopic precession of the front wheel.', "The kind of sad answer is that we don't really know for sure. The gyroscopic effect is a common answer, but tests have been done to try and cancel out the gyroscopic effect of bikes and they are still fairly self-correcting. And the geometry is mentioned, but people have made very strangely shaped bikes that we can still make work like bikes with relative ease. It seems that each of the working theories on how bicyclesmotorcycles stay up has something to do with it, but there's still some mystery there.,A moving object will not fall over. Most of the inertia in a moving bike is going in the direction which it is moving. feeding a magma chamber in the crust (which doesn't necessarily erupt too often). The Yellowstone hot spot feeds the magma chamber in the crust above for instance, though that hasn't erupted in well over half a million years. The other important point about hot spots is that they can occur anywhere within a tectonic plate. The vast majority of volcanism is associated with plate boundaries, as certain processes that occur there fuel eruptions. Hot spots are associated with mantle plumes, whose positions are not dictated by tectonic plates, and may originate from as far down as the boundary between mantle and (outer) core. With regards to ash, this is pyroclastic fire-broken material with a grain size of 2mm. Pyroclasts or tephra (interchangeable, they both refer to all sizes) are the fragments of rock and glass that are produced by more explosive volcanic eruptions, often also called tephra. Due to their small size, volcanic ash particles cool and solidify almost instantaneously upon eruption into the air. So what makes an eruption explosive? This is almost entirely down to the volatile content of a magma (chiefly water, but also carbon dioxide, sulfur dioxide and some other minor ones). Without this, any magma would erupt as an effusive one, in which molten rock would dribble down the flanks of a volcano or fissure at various speeds, or at best create a lava fountain a few metres high. The thing about volatiles like water is that in a magma chamber they are confined by the pressure of the overlying crust (they are usually 1-10km deep) and so they are dissolved within the magma, minding their own business. If some of the magma starts rising then the pressure will decrease as it nears the surface, volatiles will change phase to a gas (with a large volume expansion) and coalesce to form bubbles. If the magma ascent is rapid enough and the bubbles are forming vigorously, there comes a time when individual bubbles cannot be considered in isolation - they interact with one another, making the magma more like the foam on top of a beer than a simple fluid. In eruptions with a sudden release of a lot of pressure, this all happens extrmely quickly and the magma is literally torn into little fragments which we call ash if they are erupted at less than 2 mm diameter. That build up and sudden release of pressure doesn't happen explosively enough to form ash in all eruptions though. Stromboli, the lighthouse of the Mediterranean has a fairly high water content in its magma, but the frequency of eruption (every half an hour or so) prevents pressure building up, and the composition of the magma is thin enough to permit easy separation of bubbles from the melt. So we end up with bubbles, snaps and impressive lava fountains, though they are modest by a volcano's standards. Viscosity, or'thickness' of a magma is controlled by temperature (lower temp more viscous) and chemical composition (higher silica content more viscous). It just so happens that magmas higher in silica melt at lower temperatures, and so they form the most viscous ones. They also tend to produce the typical large conical volcano form of most people's imagination, which produces significant overburden on a magma chamber, and previous eruptions may leave behind some of the most firmly emplaced volcanic'plugs' or sealed conduits from magma chamber to surface. All of this means that magma which is high in silica, low in temp, high in volatile content, and having to overcome a large overpressure, will eventually do so in explosive fashion, creating large volumes of ash and other pyroclastic material. These are the most dangerous type of eruptions due to their immediacy, scale, and hazards for aircraft and local residents. Pyroclastic density currents are what happens when the eruption column collapses and rolls down the side of a volcano at hundreds of km per hour and many hundreds of deg C. This is what spelled instant death (and subsequent preservation) for the residents of Pompeii in 79 AD.,To quote the beginning of the [wiki article on Volcanic ash] (URL0) Volcanic ash consists of fragments of pulverized rock, minerals and volcanic glass, created during volcanic eruptions and measuring less than 2 mm (0.079 inches) in diameter.[1] The term volcanic ash is also often loosely used to refer to all explosive eruption products (correctly referred to as tephra), including particles larger than 2mm. Volcanic ash is formed during explosive volcanic eruptions when dissolved gases in magma expand and escape violently into the atmosphere. The force of the escaping gas shatters the magma and propels it into the atmosphere where it solidifies into fragments of volcanic rock and glass. Ash is also produced when magma comes into contact with water during phreatomagmatic eruptions, causing the water to explosively flash to steam leading to shattering of magma. Once in the air, ash is transported by wind up to thousands of kilometers away.

Wearing sunglasses and closing your eyes acts to reduce this confusion by removing input from the eyes.

## What is an Axiom?

An axiom is a statement that is assumed to be true, and is used as a starting point for further reasoning and arguments. In mathematics, axioms are the fundamental building blocks upon which entire systems of logic and geometry are constructed. They are considered self-evident truths and do not require proof, as they are accepted as given in the context of a particular system. Axioms serve as the foundation for deriving theorems, which are statements that can be proven to be true based on the axioms and previously established theorems.

becomes sharper. This is because of the phenomenon called pinhole effect

Pinhole cameras are simple devices that don't require any lens to produce an image. They use a tiny hole or pinhole to allow light to enter and project an inverted image onto a surface. This happens because light travels in straight lines and, when passing through a small opening, the light rays intersect, forming an image.
The same principle applies when you squint. Your closed eyelids act as a crude pinhole, reducing the size of the aperture through which light enters your eye. This reduction in light allows your eye's lens to focus the light more precisely, resulting in a sharper, more distinct image of the object you are looking at.

Squinting essentially creates a simplified version of a pinhole camera within your eye, improving image clarity in certain lighting conditions. This is particularly noticeable in bright sunlight or when trying to focus on a bright object with a less defined outline.

So, in isotonic solutions, the concentrations are balanced and the cell has no net gain or loss of water. In hypotonic solutions, there is a higher concentration of water outside the cell, meaning the cell gains water. Water will constantly leak in through the cell membrane until the internal and external pressure balances out. In a lot of cells, there's a membrane which forms a strong wall (or cell wall) pressing against the cell membrane, called turgor pressure. Because it's strong, the cell begins to swell. If you think about the structure of a typical plant cell, they have very thick and strong cell walls, so when their cells gain water in hypotonic environments, they don't necessarily burst as animal cells might do. Because of this turgor pressure, they get rigid and firm. These are very good characteristics for a plant to have.

What happens if you shock someone that's not having a cardiac arrest?
Some of the myths surrounding an AED are that if you shock someone with it, it stops them from beating. "Myth": You can’t shock someone who doesn’t need to be shocked.
Can a defibrillator start a heart that has stopped?
If the heart's rhythm is shockable, the defibrillator may be used to help restore a normal heartbeat. A shockable rhythm is one of two types: ventricular fibrillation or pulseless ventricular tachycardia. These rhythms cause the heart to quiver and cannot pump blood effectively.
Can an AED restart a heart that's been stopped?
An AED analyzes the heart rhythm and delivers a shock only if necessary. The shock delivers an electrical current to the heart, allowing it to reset. If the heart goes into a shockable rhythm, the AED can restart it.

you is heatstroke. Heatstroke occurs when the body's temperature regulation systems fail and the body temperature rises to dangerous levels. This can be caused by exposure to high temperatures or exertion in hot weather, and it's a serious medical emergency that requires immediate treatment.
When you go from a cold environment to a hot one, your body is not prepared to handle the sudden temperature change. The blood vessels that are constricted in the cold begin to dilate rapidly in the heat, which can lead to a drop in blood pressure and a decrease in blood flow to the brain. This can cause symptoms such as dizziness, confusion, and loss of consciousness.
Additionally, the sudden change in temperature can put a strain on the heart as it tries to adjust to the new conditions. People with pre-existing heart conditions are particularly at risk during this transition because their hearts may be unable to handle the sudden increase in workload. This can lead to a heart attack or other cardiovascular complications.

So, while habitus is not a direct part of the scientific method, it is an important concept that many scientific theories use to help explain social phenomena and human behavior.

When light enters your eye, it passes through the cornea and the lens. The lens bends the light rays so that they focus on the retina at the back of your eye. However, the lens isn't perfect -- its shape can vary slightly, causing the light rays to focus slightly in front of or behind the retina. This is called spherical aberration and is the reason why your vision might not be perfectly clear in all parts of your visual field. When torque is applied to change the axis of rotation it produces a reaction torque which is exerted by the spinning part on the environment (the turntable). The bearing bushings in the turntable support the weight of the turntable. They are very small, low-friction ball bearings. Side force is transmitted to the walls of the bearing housing. If there were no reaction torque then the ball bearings would not deform and thus support the weight of the turntable. If they did deform, the result would be sliding no bumping. Clearly there is a reaction torque.

Instead, it works during a specific phase of an abnormal heart rhythm: Your heart needs an electrical signal to let it beat normally, which happens in a set pattern. However, sometimes the electrical signals from your heart beat chaotically and too quickly. This means your heart doesn't have time to refill with blood between beats, which deprives the rest of your body of oxygen-rich blood. When that chaotic electrical activity becomes the primary rhythm of your heart, the condition is known as "ventricular fibrillation." If not treated quickly, it will quickly lead to death. With a shock from a defibrillator, the chaotic electrical rhythm stops. Then your body's natural pacemaker has a chance to re-establish a normal rhythm. Intrigued? its own without constantly accelerating it. To climb up to geosynchronous orbit, you do need to accelerate strongly. Is the ISS accelerating constantly? Yes, constantly. In orbit, an object is always falling towards Earth, but it's also moving sideways very fast—fast enough that it keeps missing the planet. The result is a constant state of freefall. When you're on the ISS you're falling around the Earth. Relative to the Earth, you are actually falling towards it and accelerating. However, you are also moving sideways very fast. As a result of both you falling towards it and you moving sideways very fast, you fall around the Earth instead of straight into it. Anything that is not moving sideways fast enough to fall "around" the Earth will fall straight down towards it and hit the planet's surface. Relative to the Earth, the ISS isn't constantly accelerating – it's constantly falling in a certain pattern. And relative to the spacecraft, the Earth isn't constantly accelerating – it's constantly falling in the same pattern.

"frames". A frame-rate is how many cars come off the manufacturing line per second. Now, your monitor should ideally have the same refresh rate (the rate at which it displays those frames - or cars) as the frame rate. If you tell the populace you make 90 frames per second, but your monitor displays only 60 cars per second, you'll have a bottleneck and people will be waiting around, saying, "where is the frame?". So, you can have high quality (better looking cars), but low quantity (frame rate), or high quantity (frame rate) with a bit of compromise on car quality (resolution). Or you could have both and some people are getting impatient because some cars are extra fancy, meaning it takes longer to make them. Hence, the game looks great, but looks choppy because not enough frames are being rendered at that quality level for it to be smooth for your (or anyone's) eyes. To smooth it out, you may have to reduce the quality - which means the cars are less fancy - until you get enough cars produced each second (rendering rate) to match or exceed the monitor's refresh rate.

Human waste is washed through two stages of screens; the first is coarse screens with big holes ( roughly 3 inches) to catch things like toys or diapers, the second are fine screens that collect material as small as nickels. After this, it goes into a primary clarifier, basically a giant settling tank where all the heavier organic material sinks to the bottom. Any lighter material, like leaves or soap bubbles, stays at the top of the water and is skimmed off. The biosolids that sink in slime and form a thick sludge are removed by giant scrapers. Secondary treatment follows, using microbes to eat other material currently floating around, and chemicals to disinfect the final water which goes back into the river or lake. The sludge has several steps to remove water and then be dewatered ( put in special trucks to have water extracted by pressure forcing it through membranes) after that, we typically have it shipped to a digester where it's put through an even more complex process that ultimately converts it to biosolids, used as fertilizer or energy sources.

The statement about the velocity of the car's front bumper is that it increases by 3 m/s in 3.8 seconds. This is a change in velocity over time, which is the definition of acceleration. However, we need to be careful with units. First, let's convert the time to seconds, which it already is. Now, the change in velocity is: \[ \Delta v = 3 \, \text{m/s} \] The time over which this change occurs is: \[ \Delta t = 3.8 \, \text{s} \] The acceleration \( a \) is given by the formula: \[ a = \frac{\Delta v}{\Delta t} \] Plugging in the values you have: \[ a = \frac{3 \, \text{m/s}}{3.8 \, \text{s}} \] \[ a \approx 0.789 \, \text{m/s}^2 \] So, the acceleration of the car, with respect to the ground, is approximately \(0.789 \, \text{m/s}^2\).

Understanding friction requires delving into the microscopic interactions between surfaces. ### Microscopic View of Friction At a microscopic level, all surfaces have an irregular and uneven texture composed of tiny ridges, valleys, and asperities. This interaction is the primary reason why friction exists and why it resists motion. ### Types of Friction 1. **Static Friction**: This is the friction that acts on objects when they are stationary.
